Adapting their construction, we show that, under ETH, deciding whether a hypergraph $\mathcal{G}$ with $n$ vertices and $m$ hyperedges has a minimal transversal of size at least $k$ cannot be done in time $n^{f(k)}m^{o(k)}$, for an arbitrary computable $f$. We transfer this bound to the following decision problem: given a dimension-at-most-$r$ hypergraph and a family of $s$ of its minimal transversals, decide whether another exists. Under ETH, this problem admits no uniform algorithm with running time $n^{f(r)}(s+1)^{o(r)}$. Under SETH, for every fixed $t \geq 2$, it admits no algorithm with running time $\poly(|\mathcal{G}|)(s+1)^c$ for dimension at most $2t$ and any $c<t$. As corollaries, the same exponent obstructions hold for the total time of any output-polynomial enumeration algorithm, with $s$ replaced by the total number of minimal transversals. In particular, polynomial delay is excluded under SETH already for dimension at most four.

title: Phakoseismology: Asteroseismology of gravitationally microlensed stars
authors: Marcus L. Marcussen, Mikkel N. Lund
abstract: Asteroseismology relies on disk-integrated photometry or radial velocities, in which geometric cancellation suppresses modes of high spherical degree ($l\geq4$). Observations are thus limited to deeply penetrating, low-degree modes, leaving the outer envelope inaccessible. We investigate whether a high-magnification microlensing event can temporarily lift this limitation by differentially magnifying the surface of an oscillating source star. We modelled the visibility of solar-like oscillations during microlensing, weighting the surface by limb darkening and the local magnification. We computed multiplet visibilities and the power distribution among azimuthal components, and built a likelihood model for recovering the 3D spin-axis orientation from resolved rotational multiplets. When the lens-source separation becomes comparable to the source's angular radius, the magnification gradient acts as a transient spatial filter that breaks the symmetry of disk integration, raising high-degree mode visibilities by up to three orders of magnitude. The same non-axisymmetric weighting makes the relative power of azimuthal components depend on both the inclination and sky-projected azimuth of the spin axis, imprinting the full spin orientation onto the power spectrum. With $5\%$ relative-power uncertainties, we recover the orientation to $σ_i=2.9^\circ$ and $σ_γ=11.5^\circ$. Microlensing thus does more than amplify distant stars: its magnification pattern enables spatially selective asteroseismology. The effect is strongest for rare close encounters and unlikely to support large samples, and the newly visible high-degree modes will overlap with rotationally split and mixed modes, complicating mode identification. Nevertheless, individual high-quality events may open a window on envelope physics and spin geometries for stars in the Galactic bulge and beyond.

title: Differentiable Task-Driven Coded Aperture Camera Design with 3D Gaussian Scene Representations
authors: Chengyang Yan, Donald G. Dansereau
abstract: Camera design heavily influences perception task performance, yet cameras are typically designed by domain experts through costly experimentation, in isolation from the tasks they serve. Existing joint-design methods either rely on differentiable simulation limited to pre-captured 2D images, restricting them to optics or image-processing pipeline design, or use non-differentiable camera simulators optimised with derivative-free or reinforcement-learning methods that scale poorly with the number of design parameters. We present a differentiable framework for jointly designing complex camera systems and downstream perception tasks. We use it to design two coded-aperture depth-from-defocus cameras, a monocular and a stereo configuration, by jointly optimising the coded aperture mask, camera parameters, and a depth estimation network end-to-end. Our framework represents scenes with 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructed from real-world captures, providing a differentiable image formation process for gradient-based optimisation over design spaces intractable for prior differentiable approaches. Results demonstrate that our differentiable method improves over existing coded aperture design and non-differentiable camera design baselines, offering a step forward in automated and principled camera design for autonomous systems.

title: Matrix-Game 4.0: Harnessing Video Models for Real-Time Playable Game Worlds
authors: Jihai Zhang, Runjia Qian, Kaiqin Kong, Biao Jiang, Puyi Wang, Siru Chen, Tianle Li, Guanjie Chen, Junyi Wu, Chubin Chen, Yuanhang Li, Kaichen Huang, Haobo Zhang, Yangguang Li, Wei Yu, Guibin Chen, Yu Cheng, Yahui Zhou
abstract: Moving from controllable videos to genuinely playable worlds requires persistent world state, executable game rules, and low-latency interaction. We outline a roadmap for the next generation of Matrix-Game that separates game execution from visual generation through an executable game harness, and introduce Matrix-Game 4.0 as the first system built on this design. A lightweight game engine maintains world state and executes interaction rules, a multimodal coding agent translates player ideas into game code and dynamic scene captions, and a renderer based on autoregressive video model transforms engine-rendered low-poly proxies into detailed visuals, conditioned on dynamic captions and memory references. This framework provides continuous guidance for visual generation and enables natural-language creation and modification of scenes and gameplay. Our renderer is trained on aligned low-poly and high-fidelity video pairs and distilled into a causal generator that generates in four-frame chunks with one or two denoising steps. Together with targeted inference optimizations, Matrix-Game 4.0 enables 480p, 60 FPS gameplay on a single NVIDIA RTX5090 with a key-press-to-display latency of 112ms. Single-step generation achieves 83FPS steady-state throughput with 18.2GiB of peak GPU memory usage. With fixed prompts, steady-state throughput also reaches 67FPS on an RTX5080 and 58FPS on an RTX5070Ti. We demonstrate customizable shooter and driving games with engine-enforced mechanics, and release code, model weights, and low-poly game assets to support research and creation of playable game worlds.

title: Mean-field limit and Vlasov equation for a Gaussian-thermostatted Lorentz gas
authors: Roberto Castorrini
abstract: We study N particles moving in a dispersing billiard under an electric field and coupled through a Gaussian thermostat. The corresponding mean-field equation is a Vlasov-type equation with specular reflection. We reformulate the equation as a fixed point problem for the time-integrated thermostat coefficient. This yields existence of weak solutions for every absolutely continuous initial datum of finite energy and, for bounded initial densities supported on velocities that are large compared with the field, uniqueness of the weak solution; under the finite horizon assumption, the upper bound on the velocities can be replaced by an exponential tail of the initial density. In these regimes, we prove convergence of the empirical measures of the particle system to the solution of the kinetic equation. In general, convergence holds along subsequences.

title: Annealed correlation and quenched noise sensitivity in biased deep neural networks
authors: Johan Jonasson
abstract: In earlier work by Jonasson, Steif and Zetterqvist (2023), fully connected deep neural networks with layers of width $n$, i.i.d.\ standard Gaussian weights, sign activations and no bias terms were shown to be annealed and quenched noise sensitive with respect to any joint probability distribution $\mathbb{Q}^{(n)}$ on the input $\boldsymbolω$ and its perturbation $\boldsymbolη$ satisfying a mild positive-correlation condition and $\mathbb{Q}^{(n)}(\boldsymbolη \in \{\boldsymbolω,-\boldsymbolω\}) \to 0$. Here we add independent Gaussian biases of the natural order and show that quenched noise sensitivity is retained over a broad range of depths, indeed under the slightly weaker assumption that $\mathbb{Q}^{(n)}(\boldsymbolω = \boldsymbolη) \to 0$. Thus, subject to the positive-correlation condition, quenched noise sensitivity holds under the minimal requirement that the perturbed input is asymptotically unlikely to coincide with the original input. At the same time, the annealed covariance remains bounded away from zero and is entirely accounted for by fluctuations in the network-dependent output means.

title: Adaptive Stopping of Streamed Reasoning for Language Model Agents
authors: JunHyeok Oh, Byung-Jun Lee
abstract: Reasoning-enabled language model agents can incur substantial computation before acting, although the reasoning needed varies across decisions. Existing stopping signals, such as confidence and intermediate-answer stability, can vary in effectiveness across reasoning models; signals obtained from hidden states or token probabilities also require internal access that may be unavailable or impractical. We introduce StreamStop, which learns model-specific stopping policies offline from prefix-level action agreement. A frozen prefix reader encodes available reasoning text for a lightweight stop head, allowing stopping without access to the reasoning model's internal signals. We construct and publicly release a dataset of agent reasoning trajectories with prefix-level action annotations. These annotations compare each prefix action with the full-reasoning reference action, enabling offline comparison of stopping rules and exact expected-return optimization of a discounted action-agreement objective. Conditioning the head on the discount factor allows the agreement-token trade-off to be adjusted at inference without retraining. In closed-loop evaluations on WebShop and ScienceWorld, StreamStop achieves higher observed success than most validation-selected fixed-budget settings while using fewer reasoning tokens than Full thinking. On WebShop with Qwen3.8-27B, it uses 42% fewer reasoning tokens per episode with similar observed task success.

title: Neural Closed-Loop Identification of Nonlinear Systems with Stability and Generalization Guarantees
authors: Laura Meroi, Mahrokh G. Boroujeni, Leonardo Massai, Giancarlo Ferrari-Trecate
abstract: Neural networks are expressive models of nonlinear dynamics, but identifying such systems from closed-loop data raises two difficulties: the feedback loop correlates inputs with measurement noise, biasing standard open-loop estimators, and the identified model must be stabilized by the data-collection controller, so that its closed-loop behavior matches the true plant's. We derive a complete parameterization of all nonlinear systems stabilized by a given controller, generalizing the classical dual-Youla parameterization to the nonlinear setting. Building on this characterization, we propose Internal Controller Identification (ICI), a computationally tractable framework for identifying potentially unstable systems while ensuring closed-loop stability by construction; in the linear case, our indirect method reduces to an open-loop identification problem, for which standard consistency results apply. The framework accommodates contextual information, letting a single certified model identify a family of systems, and supports a PAC-Bayesian training objective that, when data are scarce and prior knowledge is available, bounds the identified operator's expected prediction loss. Experiments show that ICI identifies open-loop unstable plants where uncertified baselines diverge, outperforms direct methods under weak excitation and feedback-correlated noise, generalizes zero-shot to environments unseen during training, and, with limited data, avoids the overfitting of empirical risk minimization while providing a non-vacuous generalization bound.

title: When Do Humans and Machines Truly Complement Each Other? Formal Conditions and Empirical Evidence for Human-AI Synergy
authors: Andrea Campagner, Federico Cabitza, Vincenzo Crupi
abstract: Can humans and artificial intelligence cooperate such that their combination yields greater accuracy than either agent alone? This result, termed \emph{synergy} or \emph{complementarity}, is notoriously difficult to achieve, even when both agents possess significant independent accuracy. In this paper, we present a formal framework to model human-AI interaction through the lens of reliance patterns, which characterize the joint correctness structure of human and algorithmic decisions. We derive mathematically necessary and sufficient conditions for synergy, demonstrating that its emergence depends on the ability of either agent to identify and correct the errors of the other, what we call Human and Algorithmic Correction. Beyond its theoretical contribution, the proposed framework provides a foundation for the design and evaluation of knowledge-based decision support systems, where interaction policies must dynamically integrate heterogeneous sources of expertise. We demonstrate this through the analysis of seven clinical case studies. Our empirical results reveal a ``dominance trap,'' where a strong algorithmic advantage can paradoxically inhibit synergy by eroding human corrective intervention. We also show that synergy can persist even in the presence of cognitive biases, such as automation bias, provided there is functional de-correlation between human and AI errors. These results provide a formal foundation for key concepts in the human-AI systems literature and offer actionable insights for designing interaction-centric AI systems that foster complementarity.

title: Classification of SNC $(p,k)$-planes with Hodge structures of K3 type
authors: Federico Fallucca, Matteo Penegini, Anna Ulivi
abstract: A SNC $(p,k)$-plane is a $(\mathbb Z/p)^k$-Galois cover $π\colon X \to \mathbb P^2$ with a simple normal crossing branch locus. In this setting, there exist several intermediate quotients $Y_1, Y_2,\dots, Y_{φ_{p,k}}$ corresponding to subgroups of $(\mathbb Z/p)^k$ of index $p$. We focus on the case where each $Y_i$ is either a surface with geometric genus $0$ or $1$, with at least one with geometric genus $1$. We classify all SNC $(p,k)$-planes satisfying these conditions obtaining that an extensive list of cases are minimal regular surfaces of general type with positive geometric genus. Moreover, these assumptions allow us to have strong control over the weight-$2$ Hodge structure of the minimal model of the covering surface $X$. Therefore, we also prove that Tate and Mumford-Tate conjectures hold for such surfaces. As an independent result of our methods, we obtain a classification of SNC $(p,1)$-planes with geometric genus $1$, which turn out to be precisely all K3 surfaces, and a classification of SNC $(p,1)$-planes with geometric genus $0$, which turn out to be instead rational surfaces.

title: Efficient SAM3 Adaptation for Multi-Class Semantic Segmentation via Dense Competitive Representations
authors: Wenbin Liao, Hao Zhu, Yike Ma, Hao Jiang, Feng Dai
abstract: The Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM3) has achieved significant progress in Promptable Concept Segmentation (PCS) by processing short noun phrases to generate segmentation masks with unique instance identifiers. While SAM3 excels at single-concept segmentation, it falls short in complex, real-world environments where multiple concepts must be segmented simultaneously. In particular, SAM3 typically fails to simultaneously process concepts with semantic overlap, leading to semantic misclassifications and redundant mask predictions. Moreover, as the number of concepts increases, the independent inference paradigm introduces prohibitive inference latency. To address these limitations, we propose the Dense Competitive Representations SAM (DCR-SAM) framework. By decoupling cross-modal interactions, the proposed method alleviates the inference latency. To resolve semantic misclassifications, DCR-SAM dynamically aligns textual concepts with visual representations and incorporates a dense competition head to enforce explicit inter-class competition. Furthermore, a learnable background token is applied to absorb non-target objects dynamically. These mechanisms effectively suppress overlapping predictions and generate high-fidelity masks. Extensive experimental evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed framework: (1) achieves a 2.3% $\sim$ 10.7% performance improvement over state-of-the-art methods, (2) delivers a 33$\times$ inference speedup compared to the native SAM3, and (3) exhibits strong robustness across diverse scenarios.

title: Theta Relations
authors: Rong Chen, Haigang Zhou, Xiao-Jie Zhu
abstract: Motivated by the classical quartic and cubic theta identities, we establish a product formula for Siegel--Jacobi theta series associated with rationally isometric positive-definite quadratic spaces. Our main theorem expresses a product of theta series of arbitrary Siegel degree as a finite double character sum over quotients of commensurable lattices. For the root lattice $A_2$, it yields a finite Fourier identity for cubes of cubic theta functions, a new proof of the two-variable cubic identity, and seven independent relations in degree two. A second specialization gives a new square analogue of the two-variable cubic identity. At the origin it reduces to $a(q)a(q^2)=b(q)b(q^2)+c(q)c(q^2)$; in degree two, the same seven relation patterns recur with each cube replaced by the corresponding product at $τ$ and $2τ$. We further extend the cubic identities on $A_2$ to $\ell$-th-power identities on $A_{\ell-1}$ for every $\ell\geq3$, and to $2\ell$-th-power identities on $A_{\ell-1}$ for every $\ell\geq2$, in arbitrary Siegel degree. The doubled-order construction recovers Jacobi's quartic identity and gives its analogues in arbitrary Siegel degree.

title: From Proper Scoring Rules and Edge Biases to Mumford-Shah Models: Robust Unsupervised Hyperspectral Image Segmentation
authors: Fabian Conrad, Benjamin Berkels
abstract: Hyperspectral images provide a rich representation of the underlying spectrum for each pixel, allowing for a pixel-wise classification/segmentation into different classes. As the availability of labeled hyperspectral images is limited and the acquisition of labeled training data is time-consuming, unsupervised segmentation methods are important in hyperspectral image segmentation. Spectral variability, mixed pixels, noise as well as high correlation between neighboring spectral bands make this task challenging. We present a feature-agnostic, unsupervised hyperspectral segmentation framework based on the piecewise-constant Mumford-Shah functional. Our framework turns a strictly proper scoring rule and a family of parametric probability distributions into an indicator function for the Mumford-Shah functional, and we naturally generalize some previous Mumford-Shah based models for image segmentation this way. Our focus will be on heavy-tailed elliptical distributions, the negative log-likelihood score and the score based on the beta-divergence to deal with the heavy outliers in hyperspectral imaging. Using the interplay between the calculus of variations and statistics, we also propose a robustness step to estimate the statistical parameters of these heavy-tailed elliptical distributions. In addition, an edge bias, which contains prior boundary information, is incorporated into both the data fidelity term and the perimeter term of the Mumford-Shah functional. Numerical experiments show that, to the best of our knowledge, our method achieves the highest overall accuracy among fully unsupervised methods on three of the four standard benchmarks (Indian Pines, Kennedy Space Center, Pavia University and Salinas) evaluated on the full scenes. It also improves upon our previous Mumford-Shah based model.

title: From Harmonic Oscillators to Multiplicity Distributions in Particle Production Processes
authors: Trambak Bhattacharyya, Maciej Rybczyński, Zbigniew Włodarczyk
abstract: We propose an oscillator framework of studying multi-particle production processes using the information theory approach. For a system of degenerate oscillators, we derive the negative binomial distribution (NBD) and its nonadditive generalization represented as gNBD. We observe that gNBD derived from nonadditive statistics describes data in higher multiplicity region, thereby providing an alternative for the multi-component distributions used in phenomenological studies. We also generalize our framework for non-degenerate oscillators and encounter a Lerch-type generalization of the Barnes zeta function that, to the best of our knowledge, has not been studied in the context of nonadditive statistics and multiplicity studies before.

title: Unsupervised Head Network Personalization for Split Computing via Federated Learning
authors: Yutaro Horikawa, Takayuki Nishio
abstract: Split Computing (SC) is a distributed inference method designed for balancing computational load and reducing latency by partitioning a neural network into head and tail networks and deploying them across both a mobile device and a server, respectively. Due to the limited bandwidth and computational power of mobile devices, the head network is often replaced with a neural network that requires lower computational and communication resources. However, it is challenging to prepare a sufficient quantity and quality of labeled data on the mobile device side for training the replacement head network. Furthermore, the data prepared by mobile users often contains sensitive privacy information, making data aggregation difficult. In this paper, we propose a data-efficient head network training method for SC. This method utilizes federated learning and knowledge distillation to train the head network using a small amount of non-IID and unlabeled data from mobile devices, ensuring that the training datasets are not exposed. Moreover, by introducing personalization, we enhance the accuracy to levels comparable to or exceeding those of existing methods. The experimental evaluations demonstrate that, despite data constraints imposed only on our method, it achieves accuracy comparable to the baselines. Furthermore, it significantly reduces the communication requirements by 95% on mobile devices, with only a 3-5 percentage point drop in accuracy from the original model.

title: infomeasure-rs: A High-Performance Rust Library for Information-Theoretic Measures and Estimators
authors: Carlson Moses Büth
abstract: Information theory has become a standard tool across the natural and social sciences, yet practical use is limited by estimator choice, fragmented software, reproducibility, and computational cost. We present infomeasure-rs, an open-source Rust library that brings a broad set of information-theoretic measures and estimators into one self-contained, type-safe package. It covers entropy, mutual information, conditional mutual information, transfer entropy, conditional transfer entropy, cross-entropy, and the Kullback-Leibler and Jensen-Shannon divergences, with discrete (plug-in and bias-corrected), kernel, ordinal, and nearest-neighbour estimators, including the Rényi and Tsallis families, and exposes local and global values and significance testing through a consistent trait interface. It ships as a single portable binary with no runtime dependency and is continuously validated against a reference implementation. On a single central processing unit (CPU) core, and even without its GPU or parallel paths, it is the fastest of the packages we compared across languages, matching the closest packages only for plug-in discrete entropy and substantially faster for mutual information, the conditional and transfer measures, and the kernel, ordinal, and generalised-entropy estimators. The optional GPU and multi-threaded paths accelerate selected continuous estimators further. The library is open source and, to our knowledge, the most complete information-theory package for Rust.

title: Thermal and optical signatures of a magnetic AdS black hole in dark matter and quintessence
authors: Mohsen Fathi, Marco Olivares, Carlos E. Romero-Figueroa, J. R. Villanueva
abstract: We study a static magnetic anti-de Sitter black hole surrounded by perfect-fluid dark matter and quintessence. We follow the geometry from the horizon to the observer. We first examine the horizons and curvature. We then calculate the Hawking temperature and sparsity, weak light bending, the photon sphere, the shadow, strong-deflection coefficients, relativistic images, and simple Event Horizon Telescope size intervals. Because the model has several parameters, we use a one-dimensional benchmark path labelled by $η$. The point $η= 0$ is Schwarzschild, while $η= 1$ is the selected full configuration. This path is only a clear way to present the combined changes; it is not a new coupling. We derive the main relations step by step and test the weak- and strong-field approximations with direct numerical geodesics. Along the path, the outer horizon, photon sphere, critical shadow scale, and relativistic Einstein rings move outward. A formal solar-limb comparison gives $η\lesssim 2.06 \times 10^{-5}$ if the same local environment is placed around the Sun, but this is a source-dependent analogue rather than a universal bound. With the central mass and distance values used here, the M87* diameter allows $0 \leq η\leq 1$, while the adopted Sgr A* interval gives $η\lesssim 0.665$. Longer derivations, error propagation, and numerical checks are collected in the appendices.

title: EASformer: Environment-Action-State Alignment for Industrial Generative Ranking
authors: Bohao Li, Dinglun Cao, Pengcheng Huang, Yingda Tang, Zhiting Zhao, Yi Cao, Jilei Fu, Miao Yan, Tianying Liu, Heng Chang, Bowen Du
abstract: Modern industrial ranking systems increasingly adopt generative recommendation (GR) paradigms, in which user behavior sequences and non-sequential (NS) features are tokenized and jointly modeled by Transformer-style backbones. This unified formulation provides a scalable interface for modeling long histories and heterogeneous features. However, sequence and NS representations often carry asymmetric semantics: historical representations may combine environment context with observed-action semantics, whereas candidate-side NS representations contain no observed action but incorporate richer supplementary context, such as user-item interaction features and recent behavior lists. Direct interaction between such representations can make query-key dot products compare different semantic objects, limiting meaningful cross-token interaction. To fill this gap, we propose EASformer, an Environment-Action-State disentangled architecture for industrial app ranking. EASformer constructs an explicitly aligned context environment space shared by historical and non-sequence tokens, while disentangling user actions from historical token and candidate-specific context form non-sequence tokens. Based on this aligned space, EASformer enables complementary historical action retrieval and state-conditioned action prediction. Furthermore, the disentangled design supports a Cloze-style self-supervised objective by masking historical actions and reusing the candidate prediction pathway. On an offline benchmark from a real-world industrial app marketplace, EASformer achieves an AUC of 0.89411, yielding a 0.88% relative improvement over the deployed baseline. Online A/B tests further support this advantage, with relative eCPM lifts of 1.26% and 3.94% across two real-world ranking scenarios.

title: Local Maxima of Discrete Gaussian Processes: Exact Distributions and Infill Limits
authors: Dan Cheng, John Ginos
abstract: We study local maxima of centered, unit-variance Gaussian processes observed on one-dimensional grids. For general nonstationary covariance, we give exact sitewise peak probabilities, conditional height densities, and expected peak counts using the covariance of a site and its two neighbors. The height limits established here are unified by a continuous family indexed by the magnitude of the conditional height-curvature correlation parameter $η\in[0,1]$, with a Gaussian endpoint at $η=0$, and smooth peak laws for $0<η\le 1$ with a Rayleigh endpoint at $η=1$. Under continuous covariance derivatives through total order four, we prove convergence to the smooth family and obtain corresponding intensity and expected count limits. Additional sample path and Kac--Rice regularity assumptions identify these limits with the intensity and Palm height law of continuous local maxima. For general nonstationary covariance, a necessary and sufficient increment criterion characterizes convergence to the Gaussian endpoint, including when peak probabilities vanish. Explicit finite-grid bounds control density and tail errors and yield uniform approximations across sites. For each fixed nonconstant, mean-square continuous stationary process, the fourth spectral moment gives a complete classification: finiteness yields a smooth family member, whereas an infinite moment yields the Gaussian endpoint and divergent expected peak counts on every interval of positive length. The height laws converge in total variation in both regimes. Nonstationary examples, Matérn covariance models, and numerical comparisons illustrate the results, including logarithmic boundary behavior and the distinction between distributional convergence and relative tail accuracy.

title: Inferring continuous cognitive traits from limited neuroimaging data using pairwise convolutional neural networks
authors: Marjan Rashidi, Robert Bain, Craig Stark, Jeffrey Krichmar, Mary Hegarty, Elizabeth Chrastil
abstract: Individual differences in cognitive abilities vary widely, yet the structural brain features supporting these differences remain poorly understood. Traditional brain-behavior analyses rely on predefined metrics such as volume or cortical thickness and typically assume linear relationships with behavior, limiting sensitivity in small datasets. Here, we introduce a pairwise convolutional ranking framework that learns directly from whole-brain T1-weighted MRI by making comparative rather than absolute predictions, which performs well even with small samples (N=108). We tested this method with four small-scale spatial abilities tasks. Regression analysis predicted performance with high accuracy across all tasks, achieving greater predictive power over standard regression and pointwise deep learning baselines. Iterative cortical-region removal (backward elimination) revealed brain regions supporting individual performance common to all four tasks, as well as task-specific regions. These results demonstrate that pairwise learning extracts meaningful behavioral information from structural MRI, providing prediction and interpretable insight into the neuroanatomy of individual differences.

title: PLaCA: Learning Patch-Level Future Latent Change for Action Generation
authors: Zhan Yi, Yuchen Wang, Chao Li, Lei Hong, Boyuan Yang
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but effective manipulation also requires anticipating how the environment will change. Existing world-action models explore future image prediction and latent dynamics modeling. However, generating complete future images can be computationally expensive, while highly compressed latent representations may obscure local changes. To address these challenges, we propose PLaCA, a world-to-action framework built around future latent change. PLaCA directly predicts spatially structured patch-level future latent change from the current multimodal input, preserving local information about expected environmental changes. We introduce patch-level change-aware supervision to emphasize regions undergoing larger changes and a future-to-action interface that explicitly incorporates predicted future latent change into action generation. Experiments on LIBERO-Long show that PLaCA achieves a 79.0% success rate, improving upon the Action-only baseline by 5.0 percentage points. On CALVIN, PLaCA improves the average sequence length from 2.784 to 3.564. These improvements are achieved while updating only 2.95% of the model parameters during the second training stage, demonstrating the effectiveness of future latent change modeling for downstream robotic manipulation.

title: CAESAR: Mixed Reality Search-and-Rescue Platform for Cognitive Attack Evaluation
authors: Mingyu Zhu, Jiangong Chen, Yu Liu, Hillmer Chona, Zifan Zhou, Jianan Jiang, Jonathan Dodge, Feng Qian, Mahdi Imani, Tian Lan, Gang Tan, Bin Li
abstract: Mixed Reality (MR) enables immersive training by tightly coupling virtual content with the physical environment and supporting embodied interaction. In safety-critical collaborative tasks such as search-and-rescue, however, users rely heavily on virtual elements for perception, coordination, and decision-making, making them vulnerable to cognitive attacks that subtly distort visual feedback, virtual content, or system synchronization. While prior MR security research has examined individual attack mechanisms, evaluations are typically conducted in isolated or single-user settings, and there is a lack of standardized collaborative testbeds for systematic adversarial experimentation. In this paper, we develop CAESAR, an end-to-end multi-user MR framework for systematic evaluation of cognitive attacks in collaborative search-and-rescue training. CAESAR features a modular architecture that integrates four classes of cognitive attacks within a synchronized collaborative scenario and incorporates a multimodal data collection pipeline that captures behavioral, performance, and subjective measures under adversarial conditions. We conduct a controlled user study with an in-depth analysis of the latency-based attack, demonstrating measurable effects on task performance and user behavior while characterizing users' subjective experience under adversarial conditions.

title: Corpus Quality Improves, Retrieval Utility Does Not: An Ablation of Preprocessing and Refinement in a Speech-to-QA Pipeline
authors: Wonsup Shin, Jingu Kim
abstract: Practitioners building training corpora with a pipeline of language models keep a preprocessing or refinement (post-process) stage when switching it on raises the corpus quality. We ablate a production pipeline that turns conference speech into question-answer pairs. The preprocessing stage rewrites the transcript, and the refinement stage filters the generated pairs. Switching each on and off gives four corpora from the same 40 Korean medical and finance sessions. On the corpus itself, quality rises as the stages switch on. Four LLM judges and six human domain experts rank the four corpora the same way, and the fully refined corpus leads by +0.18 and +0.22 on a 1-5 scale. We then ask whether that gain carries downstream. We supply each corpus to six models at inference and measure retrieval accuracy. The ranking does not hold. Enabling the transcript rewrite lowers retrieval accuracy by 0.061, the only stage effect that survives correction for multiple comparisons. That stage also reads the whole session, so it almost doubles the cost of one. With both stages on, accuracy does not change. An equivalence test we declared in advance confirms this. The corpus itself is clearly valuable. It lifts retrieval accuracy from 0.231 to 0.748 in every model and domain we test. More than a third of its pairs carry knowledge that neither of two frontier models produces on its own. On our data, the null does not come from weak corpora. A rising score on a rubric of this kind did not predict what the corpus holds for a model.

title: Vanishing transport noise enhances stability of stratified Couette flow in the 3D Boussinesq system
authors: Lei Zhang
abstract: In this paper, we study the enhanced nonlinear stability of stably stratified Couette flow in the three-dimensional Boussinesq system driven by a common affine Stratonovich transport noise. Our main result shows that, for fixed $β>1/2$, suitably chosen noise amplitudes enlarge the range of perturbations for which we prove stability, even as they vanish with viscosity. For each fixed deterministic Sobolev perturbation satisfying the sufficient smallness conditions, the strong solution is global and obeys stability estimates on an event of prescribed high probability. No spatial localization or vanishing initial double means are required. The proof combines noise-induced mixing with coupled energy estimates to control nonlinear feedback and preserve the physical damping of the fast vertical velocity and temperature.

title: CUA-Recovery: Benchmarking Error Recovery in Long-Horizon Computer-Use Agents
authors: Xu Hu, Haoming Li, Yuxiang Wang, Jinxin Yang, Kangshuo Li, Licheng Wang, Dingyi Kang, Jiayu Song, Tianhao Wang, Zhanhua Hu, Xu Yang, Qiannan Li, Bingzhe Li, Feng Chen
abstract: As computer-use agents (CUAs) move to long-horizon workflows spanning multiple applications, undetected errors can silently corrupt persistent state and cause cascading failures in subsequent actions. Reliable error detection and recovery have become critical bottlenecks for building robust CUAs. However, existing benchmarks focus primarily on end-to-end task performance, providing limited insight into whether agents can detect and recover from errors during execution. The few benchmarks that evaluate recovery rely largely on manually injected errors, which may not reflect the types or horizons of failures induced by real agent policies. We introduce CUA-Recovery, a benchmark comprising test and training suites across multiple desktop applications. We construct it using ReRail, a framework for synthesizing long-horizon tasks and trajectories in a persistent desktop environment. ReRail composes MyPCBench tasks into new long-horizon workflows with executable ground truth, collects verifier-confirmed failures from multiple policies, and turns them into verified recovery trajectories. CUA-Recovery comprises a human-verified test suite of 2,250 erroneous states over 100 tasks and a training suite of 8.6K trajectories over 377 tasks. Evaluation on the test suite shows that agents struggle both to recognize inherited errors and to complete the task. Across six agents and six takeover depths, Error Awareness Rate (EAR) reaches at most 44.0% and Pass@3 at most 25.5%. After fine-tuning Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on the training suite, its average EAR rises from 19.9% to 35.2% on held-out recovery states, and its Rubric Score goes from 5.0% to 16.1%. It also gains 15.3 points on MyPCBench and 10.8 points on Odysseys for Pass@3, showing that the training trajectories help both with recovery and with completing tasks from a clean start. Our code is available at https://github.com/xu-hu-2002/CUA-Recovery.

title: Secure Multimodal Federated Optimization via Hierarchical DNA-Based Key Management
authors: Yuping Yan, Yaochu Jin
abstract: Federated optimization over heterogeneous multimodal data enables distributed institutions to collaboratively optimize a shared model using medical images, genomic profiles, clinical records, and physiological signals without centralizing raw data. However, protecting modality-specific data throughout the optimization lifecycle remains insufficiently explored, particularly when heterogeneous modalities require separate encryption keys and selective local access. This paper proposes a secure multimodal federated optimization framework that separates local data protection from federated-update protection. A trusted key-management authority securely provisions one client key through Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE), from which each client locally derives modality-specific symmetric keys using the domain-separated HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF). Heterogeneous modalities are mapped into a unified DNA-domain representation and processed through a DNA-origami-inspired structural transformation before authenticated encryption with AES-GCM. During local optimization, only the required modalities are decrypted within an authorized client environment. Individual model updates are independently protected through secure aggregation, allowing the coordinator to observe only aggregated updates rather than each client's contribution. Together, these components establish a structured approach to modality-specific protection and secure collaborative optimization, integrating hierarchical key management, authenticated local encryption, and aggregation-level update protection within a unified framework.

title: The first-order part of the Ordered Variable Word theorem
authors: Ludovic Patey
abstract: An ordered $ω$-variable sequence over a finite alphabet~$A$ is an infinite sequence over the extended alphabet $A \sqcup \{ x_0, x_1, \dots \}$, where each variable kind appears at least once, and the last occurrence of $x_i$ appears before the first occurrence of $x_{i+1}$. The Ordered Variable Word theorem states that for every finite coloring of the words over a finite alphabet~$A$, there is an ordered $ω$-variable sequence~$W$ over~$A$ such that every word induced by substituting variables with letters, and cutting before the first undefined variable, has the same color. In this article, we prove that the Ordered Variable Word theorem is $Π^1_1$-conservative over $\mathsf{RCA}_0 + \mathsf{B}Σ^0_2$. It follows that the tree theorem for singletons by Chubb, Hirst, and McNicholl is $Π^1_1$-conservative over $\mathsf{RCA}_0 + \mathsf{B}Σ^0_2$, answering a long-standing open question. Lemma 3.13 was found by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic).

title: BCT: Bayes-Consistent Tempering for Flow Language Models
authors: Daisuke Oba, Hiroki Furuta, Naoaki Okazaki
abstract: Temperature scaling is typically applied as a post-hoc transformation of model probabilities. In posterior-induced flow language models, this creates two mismatches. First, posterior tempering implicitly changes both the endpoint distribution and the distribution of intermediate noisy states, while the denoiser remains trained on the original states. Second, the tempered posterior weights are combined with transport dynamics derived for the untempered flow. These mismatches are reflected empirically: lowering temperature improves GSM8K performance much less reliably in flow LMs than in discrete diffusion LMs. We introduce Bayes-Consistent Tempering (BCT), which makes temperature explicit in both the distributions and dynamics of the generative flow. Its learned realization trains the denoiser on tempered intermediate states and tempers the endpoint distribution using the corresponding tempered dynamics. We also derive training-free variants for conventionally trained checkpoints. Across hyperspherical flow LMs with two denoiser architectures and a von Mises--Fisher flow LM, BCT improves GSM8K generation across broad temperature ranges and achieves the strongest tempering performance. The gains also extend to Sudoku, demonstrating benefits on tightly constrained generation. At very low temperatures, the learned realization is also markedly more robust than the training-free variants, supporting temperature as a property of the generative flow across training and inference rather than a post-hoc probability adjustment. Code and model weights are available at https://daioba.github.io/bct .

title: Single-photon time qubit: Quantum-vacuum control and complementarity of the arrow of time
authors: Tai Hyun Yoon
abstract: Treating the arrow of time as a controllable quantum variable rather than a fixed external parameter is a central challenge in quantum physics. Recently, Bloch~\cite{Bloch2025} proposed the theoretical concept of a \emph{time qubit}, a two-level control space $\mathcal{H}_T=\mathrm{span}\{\ket{+},\ket{-}\}$ that selects between opposite Hamiltonian evolutions $\hat{H}_{\pm}=\hat{H}_0\pm\hat{V}$, but this paradigm has remained experimentally unrealized. Here we formulate the quantum-optical theory of a single-photon time qubit---uncovering quantum-vacuum control and complementarity of the arrow of time---and experimentally probe and validate its predictions using phase-resolved single-photon interferometry from two coherently seeded entangled nonlinear biphoton sources~\cite{Lee2018,Yoon2021}. First, we show theoretically and verify experimentally that a controlled $π$ pump--seed phase inversion during pair creation from the quantum vacuum flips the stimulated displacement generator $\hat{V}\to -\hat{V}$ on top of the spontaneous two-mode squeezing background $\hat{H}_0$, reversing the stimulated evolution time [$\hat{U}_{\mathrm{stim},-}(t)=\hat{U}_{\mathrm{stim},+}(-t)$] and enabling universal single-qubit $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ control and postselection-free first-order tomography on the temporal Bloch sphere. Second, we prove that spontaneous idler vacuum fluctuations record complete which-branch (temporal-direction) information whereas the shared coherent seed erases it without cascading or aligning the idler beams, establishing an exact wave--particle complementarity law $|\bm{r}|=\mathcal{V}=|α|^2/(1+|α|^2)$ for the purity of the arrow of time and enabling direct first-order measurement of the Loschmidt time-reversal echo.

title: Probing Nearby Electron Sources and Local Diffusion with the TeV All-Electron Spectrum
authors: Zhen Xie, Ruizhi Yang
abstract: Radiative losses restrict multi-TeV cosmic-ray electrons to young nearby accelerators, allowing the all-electron spectrum (electrons plus positrons) to retain information about particle release and local transport. We investigate how a nearby source can shape this spectrum using Vela as a representative example. We compare a birth-time burst with continuous release for the same total injected electron energy and examine the dependence on the diffusion coefficient, injection index, and source energetics. The burst spectrum develops a cooling-limited boundary near 28 TeV at the age of Vela, whereas continuous release produces a broader high-energy tail through the contribution of recently injected particles. The flux at Earth is largest over a finite range of diffusion coefficients, reflecting the competition between inefficient arrival and spatial dilution. Harder injection spectra and larger released energies increase the source contribution in the multi-TeV region, and we map the combinations of injection index and released electron energy that can produce an observable spectral feature. For anisotropic diffusion, the source visibility also depends on the angle between the Vela-Earth direction and the local ordered magnetic field. Future direct measurements extending the all-electron spectrum beyond several TeV could therefore distinguish different release histories and constrain both the energetics of nearby sources and local cosmic-ray transport.

title: Standards-Guided and Dependency-Aware Code-Level Documentation Generation
authors: Tingxu Han, Wei Song, Ziming Li, Yuchen Chen, Weisong Sun, Zhenpeng Chen, Chunrong Fang, Zhenyu Chen, Yang Liu
abstract: Automatically generating high-quality documentation for software repositories remains challenging: existing approaches largely treat documentation as unconstrained text generation, lacking explicit quality specifications, depending heavily on long-context prompts over raw code, and offering limited support for reproducible evaluation. We argue that code-level documentation generation should instead be a standards-guided software engineering task, in which documentation is generated and assessed against explicit, reusable quality requirements derived from authoritative standards. We define code documentation as natural-language descriptions of repository functions and classes, organized by source-code path. We present CODEDOC, a standards-guided and dependency-aware framework that identifies dependencies between code entities via static call-graph and AST analysis and constructs dependency-aware structured prompts combining local code context, repository paths, and documentation criteria drawn from authoritative standards and style guides. We further introduce an interactive LLM-as-a-judge protocol that supplies criterion-aligned feedback to refine generated documentation along fine-grained dimensions from formal and practice-oriented standards. Experiments on ten open-source Python repositories show that CODEDOC produces higher-quality documentation than RepoAgent and a long-context baseline under standards-aligned evaluation, with relative improvements of 11.6%-17.0% and 21.4%-29.6%, respectively, while consuming roughly an order of magnitude fewer tokens per documentation entity than the long-context baseline. A human study confirms substantial alignment between LLM-based and human judgments (Spearman's rho = 0.72), and the relative findings hold across different judge LLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/ControllableModel/CodeDoc.

title: A Two-Way Street: Surveying the Interplay between Code-Mixing and Native Languages in Text and Speech
authors: Debajyoti Mazumder, Akash Anil
abstract: Systems for code-mixed (CM) text and speech rarely start from scratch. CM data is scarce, so most work borrows from the languages being mixed, which we call native languages. This transfer can also run in reverse, when CM data is used to improve models for the native languages. Existing surveys focus on processing CM itself, and none brings the two directions together. This paper fills that gap with a systematic survey of transfer in both directions, across text and speech. We organise the surveyed work in a taxonomy of transfer direction, route and modality. Through this taxonomy, we find that most transfer runs from native languages into the CM setting. The reverse direction is younger, and in it code-switching mainly helps by aligning the two languages. Text and speech work share methods but rarely cite each other. On a shared speech benchmark, native data helps more than new architectures. These findings point to open challenges, such as how much native and CM data to mix in training, and how to evaluate CM text written in different scripts.

title: Terracini loci of tangential varieties of Veroneseans
authors: Douglas A. Torrance
abstract: The Terracini locus of a projective variety tells us the sets of points at which Terracini's lemma will fail to recover the dimension of the corresponding secant variety. We study the Terracini loci of tangential varieties of Veronese varieties, classifying several cases, including a complete classification of the Terracini loci of tangential varieties to rational normal curves. We also show that many Terracini loci involve only sets with "intratangent pairs" that lie on the same tangent space to the underlying Veronese variety. Finally, we give some applications to algebraic statistics, showing that osculating varieties of Veronese varieties are moment varieties for local mixtures of location families and connecting Terracini loci to local identifiability.

title: A Radiation-Hardened, Fault-Aware Quantized Neural Network That Self-Heals
authors: Peter Xiangyuan Ma, Joshua S. Bloom
abstract: Deep learning (DL) models are increasingly being deployed into radiation-challenging environments in spacecraft, particle accelerators, and, soon, space-based data centers. Instantiated as a learned orchestration of numbers stored in persistent memory, models are susceptible to continual degradation as high-energy particles corrupt data. At inference time, new data passed through the network fundamentally break the off-line assumptions and guarantees of a static model determined during training. To preserve the quality and efficacy of the models, fault tolerance against bit flips is a clear objective. In this work we developed a runtime method for repairing the quantized weights of neural networks (NNs) after bit flips on commodity, commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) hardware, without storing extra replicas. Our work extends the well-established Fault-Aware Training (FAT) paradigm by adding an alignment penalty to concentrate undamaged activations and weights into a low-rank subspace, and we then reconstruct flagged corrupted coordinates from the uncorrupted survivors. We call this method {\it Projection Healing} and apply it to six regression benchmarks on quantized NNs. Holding a FAT checkpoint fixed and toggling only the runtime heal gives a further ${\sim}23\%$ reduction in the native-unit excess integral. Across those datasets the method extends the operational scrub interval by a median of $2.04\times$ at a $+5\%$ RMSE degradation and $1.96\times$ at $+50\%$, compared with $1.62\times$ and $1.07\times$ for classical Single Error Correction, Double Error Detection (SECDED). This introduces a new path towards designing resilient data-driven models, complementing established hardware redundancy, ECC, and FAT-based techniques.

title: Learning Inter-Graph Interactions Between Heterogeneous Substructures of Chemical Systems
authors: Gyoung S. Na
abstract: Complex chemical systems containing heterogeneous substructures are common in real-world applications. Various physical phenomena of the complex chemical systems are derived from the interactions between the heterogeneous substructures. However, existing graph representation learning methods for inter-graph interactions assumed graph-level interactions between homogeneous structures, such as organic molecules and inorganic crystalline materials. We propose a data descriptor of the complex chemical systems and a graph neural network for learning inter-graph interactions between organic and inorganic compounds. We applied the proposed method to predict the physical properties of hybrid solar cell materials containing heterogeneous substructures, which have received significant attention for sustainable energy resources. By learning heterogeneous inter-graph interactions, the proposed method achieved state-of-the-art accuracy in predicting band gaps of 1,682 hybrid solar cell materials.

title: WaveSpec: Multi-Spectral Iris Presentation Attack Detection via Wavelength-Conditioned Spectral Coherence Adaptation
authors: Raghavendra Ramachandra
abstract: Multispectral iris presentation attack detection benefits from observing the same iris across multiple near-infrared wavelengths, but existing methods often use wavelength information mainly for conditioning or fusion. This can limit their ability to explicitly model whether the spectral response of a sample is coherent across bands. In this paper, we propose \textbf{WaveSpec}, a multispectral iris PAD framework that performs feature-level spectral coherence adaptation. Each NIR band is first encoded with a DINOv2 backbone. The proposed Set Conditioned Spectral Coherence Adapter then updates each band feature using the consensus of the available spectral set, the band-specific deviation from that consensus, and wavelength identity. The adapted features are projected into structural, spectral, and anomaly representations, adaptively pooled, and classified as bona fide or attack. We evaluate WaveSpec on the MSIrPAD benchmark under a strict cross-artefact protocol, where the model is trained with one presentation attack instrument and tested on unseen attacks. WaveSpec reduces the average D-EER from 8.45\% for SpectraIrisPAD to 3.33\%, and reduces average BPCER@APCER=1\% from 43.16\% to 12.07\%. Ablation results show that the SCSA adapter and spectral residual are central to the improvement, while a band-subset analysis shows that WaveSpec remains effective under partial spectral observations and performs best when all five bands are available. The method adds only modest computational overhead, with 11.15 ms end-to-end latency per five-band sample on an NVIDIA L40S-48Q GPU.

title: HiQGS: Hierarchical Spatiotemporal Querying for Feed-Forward Gaussian Reconstruction
authors: Qiaowei Miao, Qifeng Cheng, Yijing Guo, Yuru Xiao, Ziqian Ni, Sheng Yang
abstract: Feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction from sparse posed monocular frames requires reasoning over observations that vary jointly in viewpoint and time. Existing methods either predict Gaussian primitives from observation-aligned features or aggregate multi-frame information through compact latent queries. However, the former tightly couples Gaussian allocation to individual frames, while the latter does not explicitly structure observed evidence according to its temporal relation to the requested timestamp. Consequently, evidence across spatial scales, viewpoints, and timestamps can be difficult to align and integrate. We present \textbf{HiQGS}, a query-based hierarchical framework for feed-forward Gaussian scene reconstruction from sparse monocular frames. HiQGS introduces a \textbf{Hierarchical Spatiotemporal Encoder} that organizes multi-resolution geometry-appearance visual features according to image location, observation time, and camera pose, thereby preserving complementary appearance and structural cues. Our \textbf{Time-Adaptive Decoder} use target timestamp queries the resulting hierarchical representation to retrieve relevant spatiotemporal evidence and predicts the corresponding Gaussian scene state. Experiments on static and dynamic scene reconstruction benchmarks demonstrate strong rendering quality and geometric accuracy, validating the effectiveness of hierarchical visual encoding and target-time-aware Gaussian querying.

title: Functional meta-analysis of survival curves across reporting formats and time points
authors: Keisuke Hanada
abstract: Meta-analyses of survival outcomes commonly pool log hazard ratios or survival probabilities at selected time points. When reporting formats and observation times differ across studies, methods are needed to use available survival information for estimation at a common target time. We propose a functional random-effects model on the complementary log--log scale that synthesizes Kaplan--Meier curves and survival probabilities at discrete times as functional data. Studies that do not report survival at the target time contribute to its estimation through the use of their observed curves to estimate group-specific mean functions. The estimated between-group contrast is interpreted as a log hazard ratio under proportional hazards and as a time-specific log cumulative hazard ratio under non-proportional hazards. In simulations with delayed effects and crossing survival curves, the root mean squared error for the log cumulative hazard ratio was lower than that of the two-stage Cox method, and interval coverage was close to the nominal level. In an application to disease-free survival in resectable non-small cell lung cancer, the two-stage Cox method estimated an average hazard ratio, whereas the proposed method captured nonlinear changes in the cumulative hazard ratio over time.

title: Meta Expert: Cross-Layer Expert Sharing for Storage- and Retrieval-Efficient MoE
authors: Ermo Hua, Xiangyu Hong, Baiting Wu, Che Jiang, Haozheng Hou, Yicheng Gu, Hanjing Wang, Qirui Zeng, Ming Zhang, Ning Ding, Qipeng Guo, Youbang Sun, Biqing Qi, Bowen Zhou
abstract: As model parameters scale up, sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches have become essential for model scaling. However, mainstream models currently adopt hierarchical architectures, where experts in different layers, although topologically independent, exhibit substantial similarity and redundancy in their stored content. Compared to the hierarchically arranged \textbf{Local Expert} in existing mainstream models, we hypothesize that inter-layer shared \textbf{Meta Expert} hold greater potential. To this end, we conduct a multi-dimensional empirical comparison between Local and Meta Experts, and find that models incorporating Meta Experts exhibit lower parameter redundancy, together with lower cross-entropy loss and higher downstream task accuracy. With the activated quantity and the expert granularity held fixed, \textbf{our model matches the performance of Vanilla MoE using only 70--80\% of the experts}, substantially improving the model's scaling potential. Beyond removing inter-layer redundancy among experts and improving information storage efficiency, our theoretical analysis further shows that, compared with Local Experts, Meta Experts provide hidden states with more flexible residual pathways, thereby improving information retrieval efficiency.

title: Benefit and Cost of Random-Token Replacement under Repeated Data: A Known-Entropy Decomposition and Evidence from Ten Real Corpora
authors: Wonsup Shin, Jingu Kim
abstract: When unique pretraining data is scarce, models see the same tokens many times and are thought to memorize. Random-token replacement, an input-corruption augmentation, is one remedy reported to lower validation loss, but a lower loss alone does not reveal which source of error it reduces. On a controlled source whose entropy rate is known in closed form, we show that replacement shrinks predictions toward the corpus average. We also introduce a decomposition that separates validation loss into approximation, estimation, and memorization terms. This shrinkage view predicts that replacement's bias cost needs no memorization but its benefit does. Memorization raises validation loss after its minimum, so we report the effect at two points, the minimum validation loss and the end of a fixed budget. Where replacement helps, it reduces this rise by about 60%. At the end of the budget, it turns from harmful to helpful as the controlled source becomes less predictable; at the minimum, it helps at no predictability level under the fixed recipe. On Korean and Japanese web text, replacement removes about a third of the loss rise after the minimum by the end of the budget, but its effect at the minimum is much smaller. Across ten real corpora, replacement lowers the final loss on nine. It harms only the census corpus, program-generated JSON that is the most redundant of the ten and much more redundant than any of 64 further prose and code corpora we measure.

title: Beyond Experience: Knowledge-Guided Evolution for NPU Kernel Generation
authors: Xi Chen, Ming Shen, Haotian Yan, Ruoyu Sun, Tianjun Yao
abstract: LLM agents have become capable kernel engineers on mainstream GPU stacks, but they struggle on emerging accelerators such as Ascend NPUs, whose programming model is barely represented in pretraining data. Recent NPU agents address this gap largely through experience: they accumulate memory from their own generation and optimization trials and reuse it on later tasks. We argue that experience alone is not enough for kernel generation. An agent can only remember what it has tried, and it rarely tries a mechanism it does not know. As a result, such memory offers little help when a new operator calls for a different mechanism, and even familiar operators raise unseen situations as optimization proceeds. We present ASCENDEVOLVE, which grounds every step of an evolutionary kernel search in a large external knowledge base built from platform documentation, toolkit headers, and operator repositories. Because this corpus far exceeds any context window, ASCENDEVOLVE indexes it and routes each agent to a small, task-specific slice of evidence instead of the corpus itself. The retrieved knowledge seeds diverse implementation strategies, guides repair when a candidate fails, and constrains how strong candidates are recombined. On 53 Ascend C operators from CANN-Bench spanning four difficulty levels, ASCENDEVOLVE achieves an overall score of 71.39, improving over Reflexion and OpenEvolve by 11.6% and 17.2%.

title: DuplexLedger: Benchmarking Transactional Memory in Full-Duplex Speech Agents
authors: Yuxuan Li, Xiangchen Guan, Kunrong Li, Jin Wang, Kaiwen Luo, Yang Xiao, Yufei Guo, Zhisheng Chen, Liang Lin, Kun Wang
abstract: Full-duplex speech agents must update persistent memory while listening and speaking, yet it remains unclear which events should be stored, revised, or excluded. Existing benchmarks isolate interaction timing from memory outcomes, obscuring the state transitions behind a correct answer. We introduce DuplexLedger, a bilingual benchmark of 1,094 persistent sessions aligning four full-duplex scenarios with event-level Write/Update/Ignore/Retain supervision, explicit pre/post memory states, and 6,564 same-session questions and checks. Evaluating five full-duplex models reveals an interaction-memory gap: no system combines strong boundary control with coherent final-state memory, and the best final-state fact coverage is 2.01%. We propose ACT-Mem, an 8.92M-parameter sidecar comprising an event controller, a versioned transactional ledger, and a typed retriever coupled with a frozen MiniCPM-o 4.5 backbone. On 219 held-out sessions, ACT-Mem increases latest-value accuracy from 4.11% to 8.68% while reducing stale assertions and distractor adoption. It improves interaction boundaries but slows interruption stopping. These results motivate selective, auditable full-duplex memory rather than indiscriminate transcript retention. Code is available at https://github.com/lyx-researcher/DuplexLedger.

title: Factual Access States in Diffusion Language Models: From Mechanism to Knowledge Editing and Retrieval
authors: Yuchen Guo, Zhuoyuan Mao, Yiwen Guo
abstract: Factual recall is a lookup: some representation inside the network serves as the key, and what that key is made of decides which queries can retrieve the fact, what an edit must cover, and what a retriever can read. We call it the factual access state. In autoregressive (AR) models the subject position enriches attributes largely independently of the relation, and relation-specific selection happens later, at the readout position. In masked diffusion language models (DLMs) we find the state is assembled differently, and much earlier: in the first attention layer the wording of the relation is routed into the position of whichever entity is visible and the early feed-forward layers look the fact up on this fused representation. The state therefore varies with the relation's surface form and with the query direction, so the queries about one fact occupy a region of state space rather than a point, and an operation on the fact succeeds only for queries that enter it. We treat the state as an interface to a DLM's factual knowledge, and put it to two uses. Writing to the state gives a knowledge editor: from one declarative statement, Multi-View Edit fits one shared value per direction across that region and installs it in the early-MLP block, preserving source-prompt reliability while substantially improving paraphrase and reverse question answering, where AR editors gain near zero. Reading it suggests a complementary use: the state at each entity position can serve as a relation-specific retrieval vector with no training, returning both pieces of evidence for two-entity queries on which pooled, prompted and lexical retrievers almost never return both.

title: Regular Reissner--Nordström--de Sitter Black Holes: Thin-Shell Matching and Modified Density Profiles
authors: Reza Saadati, Yu Shi, Vitalii Vertogradov
abstract: We investigate two distinct approaches to regularizing the central singularity of the Reissner--Nordström--de Sitter geometry. In the first approach, a de Sitter interior is matched to an exact Reissner--Nordström--de Sitter exterior across a timelike dust shell. Using the Israel junction conditions, we derive the effective potential governing the shell dynamics and analyze its static equilibrium and radial stability. We show that radial stability requires $Λ_->Λ_+$, while the additional requirement of three distinct exterior horizons, with the shell located inside the inner horizon, leads to the stronger analytical result that such stable black-hole configurations exist if and only if $Λ_->3Λ_+$. We also derive an upper bound on the exterior mass parameter and recover the Reissner--Nordström limit as $Λ_+\to0$. Although the singular center is replaced by a regular core, the stationary exterior geometry remains unchanged, demonstrating that exterior geometric observations alone cannot determine whether the black-hole interior is singular or regular. In the second approach, we modify the divergent energy-density profile and reconstruct a smooth geometry with a de Sitter core while preserving the Reissner--Nordström--de Sitter asymptotics. Regularity fixes the smoothing scale to $β=Q^2/(2m)$, leaving no independent regularization parameter. The two constructions thus provide distinct regularization mechanisms, rather than equivalent descriptions of the same spacetime.

title: Two Is Enough: Binary Classification Priors Suffice for Multi-Class In-Context Tabular Prediction
authors: Zhixiong Cheng, Shiyuan Han, Jingjing Suo, Zhengli Wang
abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) pretrain a transformer on large-scale synthetic priors so that a single forward pass yields zero-shot tabular prediction. TabICLv2 samples the class count of its classification prior during pretraining, and the prevailing configuration caps it at ten. We report a counter-intuitive result: setting this cap directly to two---making every pretrained classification task binary---still yields weights that perform zero-shot K-way classification 2. On the 38 TabArena classification datasets (200 bootstrap rounds, anchored at default RF = 1000), the binary two-stage recipe reaches 1590.1 Elo, above the official default at 1568.0 (+22.1), above TabPFN-v2.6 (1577.1) and RealTabPFN-v2.5 (1521.6). A production-scale validation on 60 real-world credit-scoring institutions independently confirms the direction: the same checkpoint improves test AUC on 44 of 60 institutions (paired Wilcoxon p = 0.0007 for AUC, p = 0.0002 for KS) at +1.5 inference cost. Mechanistically, classification in TabICLv2 is carried not by a fixed-cardinality output head but by an in-context comparison operator matching query-row embeddings against class-conditional embeddings, so the cardinality of the output space is set by the labels present in the context, not by the label space seen during pretraining. This makes a binary prior structurally cheaper to generate and cache than a ten-class prior, demotes "number of classes" from an architectural constraint to a tunable hyperparameter, and points to a class-count-agnostic regime of TFM pretraining.

title: Exploring Recurrent-Depth Language Models for Multitask Clinical Text Processing
authors: Xi Yang, Guodong Liu, Cheng Peng, Kaleb Smith, Yingying Zhang, Xing He, Yi Guo, Jiang Bian, Haoteng Tang, Yonghui Wu
abstract: Clinical natural language processing includes diverse tasks such as information extraction, classification, and question answering. Developing one model for all tasks could simplify deployment and improve knowledge transfer. We evaluated whether small recurrent-depth language models can meet this need through joint fine-tuning and compared their performance with standard transformers. We fine-tuned Ouro1.4B-Thinking, Ouro-2.6B-Thinking, HRM-Text-1B, Qwen3-1.7B, and Qwen3-8B on 9 datasets covering information extraction, classification, inference, and question answering, and evaluated them on four additional datasets excluded from training. Across these 13 datasets, Ouro-1.4B-Thinking achieved higher performances than Qwen3-1.7B on 11 datasets; Ouro-2.6BThinking was competitive with Qwen3-8B on most tasks. Ouro models showed the largest gains on inference and question answering, whereas HRM-Text-1B showed mixed results. These findings support further study of recurrent-depth models for clinical tasks through controlled experiments to isolate architectural effects and investigate how recurrent computation influences reasoning, knowledge acquisition, and generalization.

title: AnchorRM: Parallel Intra-Batch State Reconstruction with Anchor-Based Residual Memory for Temporal Graph Neural Networks
authors: Haroon Gharwi, Kai Shu, Yue Dai
abstract: Memory-based temporal graph neural networks (TGN) rely on recurrent node memories to capture evolving interaction histories. However, temporal mini-batching introduces a trade-off between computational efficiency and temporal fidelity: when a node appears multiple times within the same batch, later interactions are evaluated using stale pre-batch memory because the intermediate memory updates have not yet been committed. This problem becomes more severe as temporal batch size increases. To overcome this challenge, we propose AnchorRM, an anchor-based residual memory mechanism that reconstructs event-specific intra-batch node states without executing sequential recurrent updates. AnchorRM treats the last committed node memory at the beginning of each batch as a pre-batch fixed anchor and uses causally preceding same-batch interactions to infer the missing state evolution relative to that anchor. The learned residual then calibrates the anchor to reconstruct an event-specific node memory for each interaction. Because each event-specific residual is predicted directly from the fixed anchor and its causal history, reconstructed states do not depend on previously reconstructed states and can therefore be computed in parallel within the batch while preserving temporal causality. Experiments across four temporal graph datasets and three memory-based backbones demonstrate that AnchorRM achieves an average 6.16x training speedup (up to 10.05x) and 28.67x batch scaling (up to 40x). These results demonstrate that AnchorRM substantially improves the scalability and training efficiency of memory-based temporal graph learning while maintaining competitive predictive performance.

title: Can Native Safety Travel? Reusing Safety Pretraining Across Models via On-Policy Distillation
authors: Bingqi Shang, Yang Zhang, Yiwei Chen, Changsheng Wang, Shiyu Chang, Bingquan Shen, Sijia Liu
abstract: Safety pretraining has emerged as a promising paradigm for embedding safety deeply into a model during pretraining, yielding robustness to subsequent fine-tuning that conventional safety post-training often lacks. We refer to this safety acquired during model pretraining as native safety. Yet native safety is expensive to acquire, confined to the model in which it was pretrained, and often accompanied by lower general utility. In this work, we rethink the practical value of safety-pretrained models and introduce, for the first time, the native safety reuse problem: Can native safety be transferred from a specialized, potentially smaller, safety-pretrained "teacher" to standard-pretrained "students," enabling them to inherit its robustness while preserving their general utility? We show that native safety can "travel" through on-policy distillation. A standard-pretrained student generates responses to safety-pretraining prompts, while a small safety-pretrained teacher supervises the student's token-level predictions along its own generated trajectories; cross-tokenizer alignment further enables transfer across model families. The resulting students exhibit substantially greater safety robustness than their safety-post-trained counterparts while retaining higher general utility than the teacher: subsequent fine-tuning raises the average attack success rate (ASR) of the 1.7B student by only 5.00%, compared with 11.58% for safety post-training, and its average utility of 48.20% far exceeds the aligned teacher's 27.42%. Unlike conventional large-to-small knowledge distillation, our framework enables selective, small-to-large safety transfer: it reuses the robust safety expertise of a smaller pretrained teacher without inheriting its utility limitations. These findings establish native safety as a reusable model property rather than one permanently tied to the originally pretrained model.

title: Timing-Aware and Interpretable Self-Attention for Event-Based Wearable Task Transition Detection
authors: Anda Ouyang, Siyuan Chen, Julien Epps
abstract: Task transition detection aims to identify when a person shifts from one task to another, providing a foundation for continuous health monitoring and timely context-aware interventions. While statistical and deep feature representations have demonstrated strong classification performance, they often rely on aggregated or latent features that are difficult to interpret in behavioural terms. Event-based features provide a compact and interpretable alternative by encoding behavioural and physiological patterns as discrete tokens with explicit semantic meaning, making them well suited for behavioural analysis in health informatics. Self-attention offers a mechanism for modelling interactions among such tokens; however, conventional self-attention classifiers primarily rely on token order and do not explicitly incorporate timing or duration information. As a result, informative temporal cues in event representations may not be fully exploited for task transition detection. This study proposes an event-based time-aware self-attention framework that represents behavioural signals as sequences of discrete events augmented with onset timestamps and durations. Event timing is encoded using a parameter-efficient kernel-based representation, while a novel type-aware duration embedding modulates information propagation according to event persistence. Experiments on a semi-naturalistic wearable dataset show that the proposed model outperforms existing event-based approaches, achieves performance beyond or comparable with statistical and deep-learning models with a more compact input representation, and provides improved interpretability through integrated-gradient-based analysis. These results indicate that explicit modelling of event timing and duration enhances both classification performance and interpretability, supporting reliable deployment in biomedical and health informatics applications.

title: Dynamical Triaxial Correlations in the Charge Radii of Neutron-Rich Ruthenium Isotopes
authors: Y. K. Wang
abstract: Nuclear charge radii are fundamental observables that track changes in nuclear structure. Recent measurements of neutron-rich Ru isotopes, interpreted using mean-field density-functional calculations, have highlighted the sensitivity of charge radii to static triaxial deformation. Whether dynamical shape fluctuations involving triaxial configurations---known to affect both nuclear ground- and excited-state properties---can reshape the charge-radii evolution remains unresolved. In this Letter, we investigate the charge radii of even-even neutron-rich $^{106-114}$Ru within a nuclear density-functional framework that combines three-dimensional angular-momentum projection with the generator-coordinate method. Including dynamical triaxial shape fluctuations yields charge radii in good agreement with experiment, without introducing additional adjustable parameters. By successively incorporating static triaxial deformation, dynamical axial shape fluctuations, and dynamical triaxial shape fluctuations, we trace how the predicted charge radii change at each step. These results demonstrate that triaxial shape dynamics can leave a substantial imprint on charge radii. They also inform the interpretation of experimental charge-radius measurements used to trace the evolution of nuclear structure, since charge radii alone cannot uniquely determine the underlying nuclear shape.

title: Less is More: Concise Retrieval and Critic-based Re-ranking for Composed Image Retrieval
authors: Yuqian Zheng, Hyoju Ahn, Hyeongjin Ahn, Eunil Park
